# File-type filtering in ripgrep

Everything that turns a flag like `--type rust` into a decision about a single
path lives in the `ignore` crate, principally `crates/ignore/src/types.rs`, with
the shipped type list in `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs` and the CLI wiring
in `crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs`. This note covers how a type is represented,
how a matcher is compiled from a set of them, and what a contributor changing
this area should keep in mind.

## How a type is represented

A file type is a `FileTypeDef` (in `types.rs`): a `name: String` and a
`globs: Vec<String>`, nothing more. The globs are ordinary shell-style patterns
such as `*.rs`, `*.{c,h}`, or `*.[chH]`, and they may also be literal file names
like `BUILD` or `alire.toml`. A definition can carry several globs, and several
definitions can share the same glob.

The shipped defaults are a flat table, `DEFAULT_TYPES: &[(&[&str], &[&str])]`,
each row pairing a list of aliases with a list of globs. One row can name a type
more than once (`(&["bat", "batch"], &["*.bat"])`), and
`TypesBuilder::add_defaults` expands the table by iterating names against globs
and calling `add` for each pair, so both aliases become independent
`FileTypeDef`s over the same globs. The table must stay sorted lexicographically
by first alias; `default_types.rs` carries a `default_types_are_sorted` test
that fails otherwise, and the file asks for 79-column wrapping.

## Building a matcher

`TypesBuilder` is the mutable staging area. It holds a
`HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>` of known definitions and a `Vec<Selection<()>>`
of what the caller asked for. `Selection` is `Select(name, _)` or
`Negate(name, _)`.

Definitions are added three ways. `add(name, glob)` appends one glob, rejecting
a name that is not all alphanumeric or that is the reserved word `all`.
`add_def(&str)` parses the two textual forms accepted from end users:
`name:glob` for a root definition, and `name:include:a,b,c` to fold the globs of
existing types `a`, `b`, `c` into a new one. The include form validates that
every referenced type already exists before mutating anything, so a bad
reference fails fast and leaves the builder untouched (the `test_invalid_defs`
test guards this). Include copies globs at definition time; it is not a live
link to the other type. `add_defaults` loads the table above.

Selections come from `select(name)` and `negate(name)`; both treat `all`
specially, expanding it to every currently-defined type. `clear(name)` drops a
definition.

`build()` compiles the `GlobSet`. For each selection in order it looks up the
named definition (returning `Error::UnrecognizedFileType` if absent), compiles
every glob with `GlobBuilder::new(glob).literal_separator(true)` into a shared
`GlobSetBuilder`, and records `glob_to_selection: Vec<(usize, usize)>` mapping
each glob's index in the set back to its `(selection index, glob index)`. It
also computes `has_selected`, true when any selection is non-negated. The result
is a `Types`.

## Matching a path

`Types::matched(path, is_dir) -> Match<Glob>` is the hot path. Types never apply
to directories, so `is_dir` or an empty `GlobSet` yields `Match::None`
immediately. Otherwise the base name is extracted with `pathutil::file_name` and
matched against that alone; combined with `literal_separator(true)`, patterns
are name-scoped and do not reach across path separators.

`set.matches_into(name, &mut matches)` fills a scratch `Vec<usize>` (drawn from a
pooled `Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>`, so calls stay cheap and thread-safe) with every
matching glob index. The highest-precedence match is the last one:
`matches.last()` indexes through `glob_to_selection` to the winning `Selection`,
and a negated selection produces `Match::Ignore` while a plain one produces
`Match::Whitelist`. Precedence therefore follows selection order, which is the
order globs were added to the set.

The `has_selected` flag drives the fallthrough. If nothing matched but at least
one type was selected, the file is `Match::Ignore` with an unmatched `Glob`;
this is why selecting Rust excludes everything that is not Rust. With no
selections, a non-match is `Match::None`. The returned `Glob` carries the
responsible `FileTypeDef` via `file_type_def()`, or `None` for the
unmatched-ignore case.

`Match` itself (in `lib.rs`) is the three-valued enum the whole crate shares. In
`dir.rs`, `Ignore::matched` calls `types.matched(...).map(IgnoreMatch::types)`
only when the matcher is non-empty; an `Ignore` short-circuits the walk and a
`Whitelist` is retained, so type filtering composes with gitignore and `--glob`
overrides under one model.

## What to know when changing this area

- Adding a shipped type means one row in `DEFAULT_TYPES`, kept sorted by first
  alias and wrapped to 79 columns; multiple aliases in a row share globs.
- Type names must be alphanumeric, and `all` is reserved.
- Globs match the base name only. Do not expect a `/` to behave as a path
  boundary here.
- Last matching glob wins. If one definition must override another, order
  matters.
- The CLI builds its `Types` in `hiargs.rs::types`: `add_defaults()` followed by
  a replay of ordered `TypeChange`s (`--type-clear`, `--type-add`, `--type`,
  `--type-not`). Behavioral changes usually belong in `types.rs`, not there.
